newsitem.title: UK: Scottish Amicable plans seen deterring bid.
newsitem.headline: Scottish Amicable plans seen deterring bid.

text.p: The plans of Britain's life assurance group Scottish Amicable to shed mutual status and float on the stock market is likely to fuel recent speculation that the group will become the target of a takeover bid.
Unveiling complex proposals for demutualisation and flotation in three to five years, Scottish Amicable's Sandy Stewart said the firm had been the subject of approaches but had had no firm offers.
And chairman Sandy Stewart said the group intended to hold on to its independence.
"Our plans do not include being gobbled up by anybody," Stewart told a news briefing.

Industry analysts said today's move would make any takeover "The policyholders are likely to get more by hanging on in there and having an interest in the future than a straight sale now. Anyone wanting to come in for them would have to make an allowance for the interest the policyholders have got," said one.
The complex structure of the proposals is also likely to prove an additional hurdle for any would-be predators.

"They'll have a fairly complicated structure with an outside shareholder, Securitas, which makes it very difficult to come in. It means that its not inconceivable, but is very hard to disturb," said Stephen Dias of Goldman Sachs.
Recent rumours had linked with Prudential Corp Plc, Dutch insurance giant ING, the Bank of Scotland and Australia's largest life assurer AMP.
The Stirling-based group is to use capital raised through the dropping of mutual status to fund a push for market share in the life and pensions industry.

It said it believed the market was entering a growth phase and that it was well positioned to take advantage of an upturn but needed capital and a more flexible structure to take advantage of the opportunities.

Exposure to the Independent Financial Advice (IFA) market - the fastest growing segment of the industry - would give it a dynamic base and would continue to be the group's focus in the future, it said.
It also plans to grow its international activities.

"In the segments they're talking about IFA, the broker market and particular policies like long term care growth rates can be quite high and the broker market has been picking up market share," said Dias.

But while the UK life market had grown very fast this year, the recovery has been from a very low base after sharp falls over the past two years and analysts said it was difficult to pick up any underlying trends.
The period before flotation is intended to allow Scottish to develop the business and the more sharply profit focused corporate culture, it said.
On flotation, it expects a premium market rating and for the group to be capitalised at around one billion pounds.

Managing Director Roy Nicolson said that there remained value to be realised in the group and that an immediate flotation would have failed to reflect the true value of the businesss and sold policyholders short.
Analysts described the proposals as a good compromise between raising some capital in the near term but not selling out too cheap.
